Organic Halide. Also called a haloalkane or alkyl halide, this is an organic compound containing one or more halogen atoms—fluorine, chlorine, bromine, or iodine—covalently bonded to a carbon atom. Because halogens are so electronegative, the carbon-halogen bond is very polar, making the carbon electrophilic and turning organic halides into prime substrates for nucleophilic substitution and elimination reactions.

Organic halides serve as the substrate for nucleophilic substitutions. They can undergo SN1 reactions through a carbocation intermediate, or SN2 reactions, which proceed in a single step with inversion of stereochemistry. They also undergo elimination reactions, either E1 or E2, in the presence of base to form alkenes. These generally follow Zaitsev's rule, producing the most substituted and stable alkene product.

These compounds act as the precursor to Grignard reagents, which are prepared by reacting alkyl or aryl halides with magnesium metal in an anhydrous ether solvent. The reactivity as a leaving group increases down the halogen group, with iodide being the best leaving group, followed by bromide, then chloride, and finally fluoride. This trend correlates with weaker carbon-halogen bond strengths and the stability of the halide anion.

Among the most notable organic halides are chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs. These volatile synthetic compounds were widely used as propellants and refrigerants until they were banned under the Montreal Protocol because they depleted the ozone layer. Chlorine is a common halogen substituent found in compounds like chloroform and polyvinyl chloride plastic. And when CFCs are photolyzed, the chlorine radicals they release catalytically destroy ozone in the stratosphere. Magnesium inserts into the carbon-halogen bond of organic halides to form nucleophilic Grignard reagents.
